title: Three perfect days in New York, from Museum Mile to the Brooklyn waterfront
dek: Three Upper East Side museums open new shows the day before you arrive, the Union Square Holiday Market is in its first weekend, and the rain should clear in time for a sunny Sunday walk across the Brooklyn Bridge.

hero.caption: The Brooklyn Bridge, best crossed on foot early on a clear Sunday morning, before the crowds arrive.

intro:
Mid-November is a good time to be in New York. The fall exhibitions are open, the holiday crowds have not yet arrived, and the city has started dressing for December without being fully taken over by it.

This weekend has a particular gift for anyone who likes museums: on Thursday, November 12, three institutions on or near Fifth Avenue open new shows on the same day. The **Neue Galerie** reopens for its 25th anniversary with Klimt's *Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I* among the works on view; the **Frick** opens a room of new paintings by the Canadian artist Kent Monkman, who takes on the Vermeer that hangs a few rooms away; and **the Met** opens a show of postwar Japanese photography, its first exhibition of Japanese photography since 1995. That makes Friday, when the National Weather Service expects rain and a high near 47°F, an easy day to spend indoors on the Upper East Side.

Saturday and Sunday look drier, partly to mostly sunny and in the upper 40s, so the plan moves outside: the Greenmarket and the newly opened Holiday Market at Union Square, lunch in the West Village, the High Line before dark, and a late set at the Village Vanguard. Sunday crosses the river on foot for coffee in Dumbo, coal-oven pizza, chamber music on a barge and dinner in a restored Victorian dining room.

Sunset comes before 5 p.m. now, so bring a warm layer and plan the outdoor parts of each day for the early afternoon.

days.title: Friday: Museum Mile in the rain
days.intro: Three museums, all opening new shows this week, and a long lunch between them, with a piano bar to end the evening.

stops.name: Café Sabarsky
stops.text:
Start in the Viennese café on the ground floor of the Neue Galerie, a wood-paneled room in a 1914 Fifth Avenue mansion. Order a coffee with whipped cream and something from the pastry case, and take a table by the window if one is free. It is the most civilized way to wait out a wet morning.

Café Sabarsky opens at 9 a.m. Wednesday to Monday and is closed on Tuesdays. It is busiest at lunchtime, so breakfast is the time to go.

stops.name: Neue Galerie: 25th Anniversary Exhibition
stops.text:
The Neue Galerie, devoted to early 20th-century German and Austrian art and design, reopened its galleries on Thursday with a show of highlights from its first 25 years. Gustav Klimt's gold *Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I* (1907) is the reason most people come, but leave time for Egon Schiele's *Town among Greenery*, Gabriele Münter's garden at Murnau and the Josef Hoffmann silver in the design rooms.

Tickets are $28; book a time online. The museum is open 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Wednesday to Monday, and the show runs to January 11.

stops.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
stops.text:
Walk four blocks down Fifth Avenue to the Met. Head first for *A Long Shadow: Postwar Japan Through the Lens*, new this week in Gallery 851. It gathers pictures by Tōmatsu Shōmei, Ishiuchi Miyako, Ishikawa Mao and others who photographed Okinawa and the towns around American bases during and after the occupation. Then pick one wing and leave the rest for another trip.

The Met is open until 9 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays and closed Wednesdays. Admission for visitors from outside New York State is $30, and the Japan show is included.

stops.name: Sant Ambroeus
stops.text:
On your way south, stop for a late lunch at the Madison Avenue branch of the Milanese pastry shop and café, which marks its 90th anniversary this year. Sit down for a plate of pasta or a salad in the dining room, or stand at the counter for an espresso and a pastry if the Met has used up most of your afternoon. It is a good, unhurried break between two museums.

Book on Resy, especially on a wet day.

stops.name: The Frick Collection: Kent Monkman
stops.text:
The Frick's mansion on 70th Street, reopened in 2025 after a long renovation, holds one of the best small collections of old masters anywhere. This week it opens *Officer and Laughing Girl* in the Cabinet Gallery: new paintings by Kent Monkman, the Cree artist, who uses Vermeer's painting of the same name, and his own alter ego Miss Chief, to look at five centuries of meetings between Indigenous people and Europeans. Afterwards, find the Vermeer itself in the South Hall.

Open 10:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., closed Tuesdays. Adult tickets are $30; book a time, since the last tickets are sold an hour before closing.

stops.name: Café Boulud
stops.text:
Daniel Boulud's Upper East Side restaurant, now at Maison Barnes on East 63rd Street, holds a Michelin star, and it is the kind of French dining room that suits a cold, wet night. The kitchen, under Romain Paumier, keeps classical technique and adds seasonal touches. Order the black sea bass wrapped in potato with red wine sauce if it is on, and the tarte Tatin for dessert. The wine list leans French.

Dinner is served from 5 p.m. on Fridays. Book on Resy and dress up a little.

stops.name: Bemelmans Bar
stops.text:
End the night in the bar of the Carlyle, where the walls are covered in murals by Ludwig Bemelmans, the author of *Madeline*, and the room is lit low and gold. A pianist plays from 5:30 p.m. and a jazz trio takes over from 9 p.m. Order a martini and settle in.

There is a music charge that depends on the artist, about $25 to $35 a person at a table and $20 to $25 at the bar. The bar asks guests to dress for the occasion: no athletic wear, hoodies, shorts or sneakers.

days.title: Saturday: Union Square, the Village and the High Line
days.intro: A market morning, a long Italian lunch, the High Line at sunset and jazz in a basement on Seventh Avenue South.

stops.name: Daily Provisions
stops.text:
Danny Meyer's all-day café, around the corner from Union Square Cafe, is where to start. The crullers are the thing: maple or cinnamon at $4.95, or one of the seasonal flavors. Add a bacon, egg and cheese ($9.50) if you need something that will last until lunch, and a coffee to carry over to the market.

It opens at 8 a.m. on Saturdays. Order at the counter; there are a few seats, but it is easy to take everything to go.

stops.name: Union Square Greenmarket and Holiday Market
stops.text:
On Saturdays the city's best-known farmers' market fills the north and west sides of Union Square from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., with apples, cider, cheese, bread and the last of the fall vegetables from farms across the region. This weekend there is a second market at the south end of the square: the Union Square Holiday Market opened on Thursday, with its rows of red-and-white stalls selling crafts, prints, jewelry and food. Shop the farmers first, then the holiday stalls.

The Holiday Market runs daily through December 24.

stops.name: Washington Square Park and the West Village
stops.text:
Walk down University Place to Washington Square Park, under the marble arch and through the park, then west into the streets of the West Village, where the grid gives up and the blocks of row houses run at odd angles. Take your time on the way to lunch: Bleecker Street, Carmine Street and the quiet stretch of Bedford and Grove Streets are all on the way.

It is about 25 minutes from Union Square to Grove Street without stops.

stops.name: Via Carota
stops.text:
Jody Williams and Rita Sodi's trattoria on Grove Street is one of the most loved restaurants in the city, and a Saturday lunch is the easiest way in. Order the insalata verde, the plain-looking green salad that people talk about for years, then the grilled octopus or fried rabbit, and a glass of something Italian. The room is small and warm, which is the point in November.

It opens at 10 a.m. on weekends. Reservations are on Resy, and walk-ins are welcome.

stops.name: The High Line
stops.text:
Walk west to Gansevoort Street and climb up to the High Line, the old elevated freight railway turned into a park. Head north through Chelsea toward Hudson Yards, about a mile and a half, past the planted beds gone gold and brown for the season and the views down the side streets to the Hudson. With sunset around 4:35 p.m., the light is low and the late-afternoon walk is the best one.

There are stairs and elevators at Gansevoort, 14th, 23rd and 30th Streets, so you can leave whenever you like.

stops.name: El Quijote
stops.text:
Dinner is in the Hotel Chelsea, at the Spanish restaurant that has been on West 23rd Street since 1930. Time Out's reviewer recommends it for dinner, and after a day on your feet a long Spanish meal in an old New York room is the right idea. Share a few plates and a bottle of Spanish wine, then walk through the hotel lobby on the way out to look at the art on the walls.

Book ahead for Saturday night.

stops.name: Village Vanguard
stops.text:
Take the 1 train two stops down to Christopher Street for the late set at the Village Vanguard, the triangular basement club Max Gordon opened in 1935. It has been mostly a jazz room since 1957, and Sonny Rollins, Bill Evans and John Coltrane all recorded live albums there. The band changes each week, Tuesday to Sunday, with sets at 8 and 10 p.m.

Buy tickets online in advance; prices vary by band, seating is first come, first served and there is a one-drink minimum.

days.title: Sunday: across the bridge to Dumbo and Brooklyn Heights
days.intro: The clearest day of the weekend, spent on the Brooklyn waterfront: a bridge, a carousel, pizza, a concert on the water and a Victorian dinner.

stops.name: Brooklyn Bridge
stops.text:
Take the subway to City Hall or Brooklyn Bridge–City Hall and walk across the bridge to Brooklyn on the raised promenade, which runs about a mile above the traffic. Early on a Sunday is the right time: the light is behind you on the Manhattan towers and the crowds are thin. Stop under the stone arches to look at the cables and up the East River.

Take the stairs down to Washington Street at the Brooklyn end for Dumbo, or keep going for Cadman Plaza. Allow 30 to 40 minutes.

stops.name: Devoción
stops.text:
Warm up at the Dumbo café of Devoción, the Colombian roaster, at Jay and York Streets. The beans come directly from small producers in Colombia and are roasted in Brooklyn about ten days after they leave the farm, much fresher than most coffee. Order a coffee made with one of the rotating single-estate lots, or a house blend if you just want something hot, and sit for a while.

It opens at 7:30 a.m. on weekends.

stops.name: Brooklyn Bridge Park and Jane's Carousel
stops.text:
Walk down to the water, where Brooklyn Bridge Park runs south along the old piers. On the way, look down Washington Street at the Manhattan Bridge framed between the old warehouses; it is the view you have seen in photographs. Then ride Jane's Carousel, a restored 1922 carousel in a glass pavilion at the water's edge, for $3.

The carousel's fall schedule is Wednesday to Sunday, 11 a.m. to 5:50 p.m. It is closed Mondays and Tuesdays.

stops.name: Juliana's
stops.text:
Patsy Grimaldi, who founded Grimaldi's, came out of retirement in 2012 to open Juliana's in the original Grimaldi's building on Old Fulton Street, with a new coal oven. Order a Margherita with San Marzano tomatoes, or the white pie with ricotta and garlic, and share a second one; the crust is thin and charred.

Lunch runs 11:30 a.m. to 3:15 p.m. Go early on a weekend to keep the wait short.

stops.name: Bargemusic
stops.text:
A few steps from Juliana's, a converted coffee barge moored at Fulton Ferry Landing has been a chamber-music hall since 1977. This Sunday at 2 p.m. the pianists Alexander Peskanov and Coady Green play a duo recital of Rubinstein, Tchaikovsky and Peskanov's own music. The room seats only a small audience, and the windows behind the players look across the river to Lower Manhattan, so you can watch the boats go by.

Buy tickets online in advance, and expect the floor to move a little.

stops.name: Brooklyn Heights Promenade
stops.text:
Walk up Old Fulton Street and into Brooklyn Heights, the city's first historic district, by way of Columbia Heights and its brownstones. The Promenade runs along the edge of the bluff above the expressway, with the full view of Lower Manhattan, the harbor and the Statue of Liberty. Arrive before sunset, around 4:35 p.m., and stay until the towers light up.

From there it is about a 15-minute walk through Brooklyn Heights to Fulton Street for dinner.

stops.name: Gage & Tollner
stops.text:
Finish in one of the grandest old dining rooms in the city, restored and reopened by chef Sohui Kim, Ben Schneider and St. John Frizell, with its mirrors, cherry wood and working gas lamps. The cooking leans Southern, a nod to Edna Lewis, who ran the kitchen in the 1980s. Order crab cakes, the fried chicken with cornmeal fritters and the coconut layer cake, and something classic from the cocktail list.

Open until 10 p.m. on Sundays. Book on OpenTable.

stay.name: The Carlyle, A Rosewood Hotel
stay.text: The Carlyle, on Madison Avenue at 76th Street, is the Upper East Side's classic grand hotel, and staying there puts you a few blocks from all three of Friday's museums. Bemelmans Bar is downstairs, so the last stop of Friday night is an elevator ride from your room.

stay.name: Hotel Chelsea
stay.text: The red-brick hotel on West 23rd Street, home over the years to writers, musicians and painters, reopened in 2022 with 155 rooms and suites full of velvet sofas and antique desks, and a top-floor spa. Time Out ranked it the best hotel in New York this fall. El Quijote, Saturday's dinner, is on the ground floor, and the High Line is a few blocks west.

stay.name: The Jane Hotel
stay.text: Built in 1908 as a hotel for sailors, the Jane has tiny cabin-style rooms of about 50 square feet, with a single bed or bunks and shared bathrooms down the hall, and larger Captain's Cabins with private baths. The old public rooms have closed, but the location, by the Hudson River Greenway and close to the High Line and the Village, is excellent for the price.
stay.wiki: American Seamen's Friend Society Sailors' Home and Institute

events.name: Neue Galerie reopens with its 25th Anniversary Exhibition
events.when: From Thu. Nov. 12; 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., closed Tuesdays
events.text: After a closure, the museum of German and Austrian art reopens all its galleries with a show of masterworks from its 25 years, including Klimt's *Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I*. Through January 11.

events.name: Kent Monkman: Officer and Laughing Girl
events.when: From Thu. Nov. 12; 10:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., closed Tuesdays
events.text: New paintings by the Cree artist, responding to the Frick's Vermeer of the same name and to the history of trade and colonization behind it. Through February 22.

events.name: A Long Shadow: Postwar Japan Through the Lens
events.when: From Thu. Nov. 12; Fri. and Sat. until 9 p.m.
events.text: Photographs from the Met's collection by Tōmatsu Shōmei, Ishiuchi Miyako and others who documented Okinawa and the base towns during and after the American occupation. Through May 2.

events.name: Union Square Holiday Market opens
events.text: The city's best-known holiday market opens for the season, with stalls of gifts, crafts and food. It runs through December 24.

events.name: Dave Matthews Band
events.text: The second of two nights at the Garden that close the band's fall tour. Expect crowds around Penn Station on Friday evening.

events.name: Bargemusic: Peskanov and Green, duo piano
events.text: Alexander Peskanov and Coady Green play Rubinstein, Tchaikovsky and Peskanov on the floating concert hall under the Brooklyn Bridge.

events.name: New York Jets vs. Buffalo Bills
events.text: A division game across the river in New Jersey. Trains run from Penn Station via Secaucus on game days; leave plenty of time.

know: **From the airports.** From JFK, take the AirTrain to Jamaica or Howard Beach and change to the subway or the Long Island Rail Road; the AirTrain is a separate fare from the subway. Allow about an hour to Midtown. From Newark, the AirTrain connects to NJ Transit trains to Penn Station. From LaGuardia, the Q70 LaGuardia Link bus runs to the subway at Jackson Heights. Taxis from JFK to Manhattan charge a flat fare plus surcharges, tolls and tip.

**Paying for transit.** The MetroCard is gone. Tap a contactless card or phone at the turnstile with OMNY; a subway or local bus ride is $3, and once you have spent $34 on the same card in a Monday-to-Sunday week, the rest of that week's rides are free. Use one card per person, since taps from different cards don't combine.

**The weather.** The National Weather Service expects rain from Thursday night into Friday, with a high near 47°F and a breeze, then partly sunny on Saturday and mostly sunny on Sunday, highs in the upper 40s. Bring a waterproof layer for Friday and gloves for the evenings.

**Closed days.** The Neue Galerie, Café Sabarsky and the Frick close on Tuesdays and the Met on Wednesdays, so none of them affects this weekend. Jane's Carousel is closed Mondays and Tuesdays. The Union Square Greenmarket runs Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays.

**Crowds.** Dave Matthews Band plays Madison Square Garden on Thursday and Friday nights, so Penn Station and the trains around it will be busy then, and the Jets play the Bills at MetLife Stadium on Sunday afternoon.
**Short days.** Sunset is around 4:35 p.m. Plan the High Line and the Brooklyn Heights Promenade for the late afternoon so you catch the light.

**Tipping and covers.** In restaurants, 18 to 20 percent of the pre-tax bill is normal; at bars, a dollar or two a drink; for taxis, 15 to 20 percent. Jazz clubs and hotel bars add a cover or music charge, and the Village Vanguard has a one-drink minimum.
